theme: Divorce; children; the rich man; Bartimaeus
readingInstruction: Read Mark 10:1-52. Teaching on marriage and divorce, welcoming children, the rich man who walked away, the third prediction of the passion, a request for places of honor, and the healing of Bartimaeus. Verse 45 is the key verse of the Gospel and the memory verse of this unit.
settingTheScene: Jesus is on the way to Jerusalem. In this chapter, he teaches on the foundations of life in the kingdom: marriage, children, wealth, and power. Each teaching reverses the world’s values. And each is followed by a picture of the cross: “The Son of Man came to serve and to give his life.” The chapter ends with a blind man who sees, just before the final approach to Jerusalem.
observation: “What therefore God has joined together, let not man separate” (10:9).
“Let the children come to me; do not hinder them, for to such belongs the kingdom of God” (10:14).
“You lack one thing: go, sell all that you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me” (10:21).
“With man it is impossible, but not with God. For all things are possible with God” (10:27).
“Whoever would be great among you must be your servant” (10:43).
“For even the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many” (10:45).
“Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me!” (10:47).
“Go your way; your faith has made you well” (10:52).
interpretation:
The Pharisees test Jesus on divorce. He points back to creation: from the beginning, God made them male and female, and the two become one flesh. “What therefore God has joined together, let not man separate.” Moses permitted divorce because of hardness of heart, but that was not God’s original design. In the house, he tells the disciples that divorce and remarriage amount to adultery. Christians have differed on how to apply this in painful situations, but the high view of marriage is clear.

Parents bring their children for Jesus to touch, and the disciples rebuke them. Jesus is indignant: “Let the children come to me; do not hinder them.” To receive the kingdom like a child, in dependence, is the only way to enter. He takes them in his arms and blesses them.

A rich man runs up and kneels: “Good Teacher, what must I do to inherit eternal life?” Jesus tests him with the commandments, and the man says he has kept them all. “And Jesus, looking at him, loved him.” Then he says, “You lack one thing: go, sell all that you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me.” The man’s face falls and he goes away sorrowful, for he had great possessions. Jesus does not make this a rule for everyone, but he exposes the idol of this man. It is hard for the rich to enter the kingdom. The disciples are astonished, and ask, “Then who can be saved?” Jesus looks at them: “With man it is impossible, but not with God.” Salvation is God’s work.

For the third time, Jesus tells them plainly what will happen in Jerusalem. And again they miss it. James and John ask for the best seats in his glory. The others are indignant. Jesus gathers them and says that the rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them, “But it shall not be so among you. Whoever would be great among you must be your servant.” Then comes the key verse: “For even the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.” The word ransom is the price paid to free a slave or captive. Jesus gives his life as the price. The “many” is a Semitic expression for a vast number. This verse is the theological center of Mark, and a statement of substitution.

At Jericho, blind Bartimaeus calls out, “Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me!” The crowd tries to silence him, and he cries louder. Jesus stops, calls him, and asks, “What do you want me to do for you?” “Rabbi, let me recover my sight.” “Go your way; your faith has made you well.” Immediately he receives his sight and follows Jesus on the way. It is the last healing in Mark, and the first time anyone openly calls Jesus Son of David. The blind man sees what the disciples cannot.
connection: Genesis 1:27 and 2:24 are the creation texts Jesus cites. Deuteronomy 24:1-4 is the Mosaic provision. Isaiah 53:10-12 says the servant makes many to be accounted righteous and bears the sin of many. Psalm 49:7-9 says no one can ransom another. 1 Timothy 2:5-6 says Christ gave himself as a ransom for all. Titus 2:14 and 1 Peter 1:18-19 speak of redemption. Philippians 2:5-8 shows his servant mind. Luke 18:35-43 parallels the story of the blind man.
application:
Memorize Mark 10:45. It is the memory verse of the unit. Say it every morning this week.

Ask what you cling to that keeps you from following Jesus fully. Pray over it.

Like Bartimaeus, call out to Jesus when others tell you to be quiet.
prayerPrompts: Thank Jesus for giving his life as a ransom for many.
Tell him what you are tempted to hold on to, like the rich man.
Ask him to open your eyes like Bartimaeus.
